query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In lightweight high‐entropy alloys, a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements promotes the formation of a continuous, adherent, and protective oxide scale (rich in elements such as Al and Cr) during high-temperature exposure, which in turn enables the alloy to simultaneously achieve low density, high mechanical strength, excellent corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance. In contrast, any micro‐segregation (e.g., copper or other elemental clustering) disrupts this oxide scale formation, leading to increased local galvanic corrosion and higher oxidation rates along with a deterioration of mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight HEA with a homogeneous microstructure and uniformly distributed alloying elements (e.g., an AlCrTiV0.5-based system) in the as-cast or solution-treated state.
generation.intervention: Induce controlled microstructural variations by processing: one set is processed to maintain compositional homogeneity and minimal segregation (via optimized thermal treatments), while a comparative set is intentionally tuned to promote elemental segregation (e.g., increased copper content or less homogenizing treatment).
generation.conditions: Both sets are subjected to high-temperature oxidation tests (in air, e.g., at 1000–1100 °C for extended durations) and electrochemical corrosion tests in a 0.6 M NaCl solution, alongside mechanical strength evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The quality and continuity of the protective oxide scale (primarily consisting of stable oxides like Al2O3, Cr2O3, and related compounds) formed on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: A homogeneous elemental distribution facilitates the rapid formation and stabilization of a dense oxide layer during high-temperature exposure, which impedes oxidative attack and corrosion and supports load-bearing performance. Conversely, micro-segregation leads to localized potential differences and discontinuous oxides that fail to protect effectively, thereby compromising corrosion and oxidation resistance and ultimately mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical testing conditions, the homogenized HEA variant will show lower oxidation weight gain, lower corrosion current densities, and maintain higher tensile strength compared to the variant with induced elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: The baseline is a homogenously processed lightweight HEA without significant elemental segregation, demonstrating optimal protective oxide formation and balanced mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism might cease to hold if the alloy is exposed to extreme temperatures or prolonged oxidizing conditions that cause spallation of the oxide layer, or if processing parameters inadvertently trigger severe microsegregation even in the nominally homogeneous alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of minor segregation on oxidation kinetics and corrosion rates remains to be fully established across different alloy compositions and service environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of lightweight HEA samples: one processed for maximum compositional homogeneity (Group A) and one processed under conditions designed to promote controlled elemental segregation (Group B). Subject both groups to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 1000–1100 °C for >100 hours) and 0.6 M NaCl corrosion tests while performing mechanical tensile tests. Use microscopy (SEM/TEM) to evaluate oxide scale continuity and grain structure.
measurements: Oxide scale microstructure and continuity (via SEM/TEM)
Potentiodynamic corrosion parameters (corrosion potential and current density)
Tensile yield strength and ductility measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples from Group B (with intentional microsegregation) exhibit similar or better oxide scale protection (i.e., equivalent or lower oxidation weight gain), corrosion resistance (similar or lower corrosion current densities), and mechanical properties compared to Group A, then the hypothesis that homogeneous elemental distribution is critical for synergistically achieving low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance in lightweight HEAs would be falsified.

A Lightweight AlCrTiV0.5Cux High-Entropy Alloy with Excellent Corrosion Resistance

Abstract: Lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of low-density, high strength-to-weight ratio metallic structural material. Understanding their corrosion behavior is crucial for designing microstructures for their practical applications. This work investigates the electrochemical corrosion behavior of lightweight HEAs AlCrTiV0.5Cux (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) in a 0.6 M NaCl solution. These HEAs were produced by vacuum arc melting. In contrast to 304L stainless steel, all of the alloys exhibited lower current density levels caused by self-corrosion, with AlCrTiV0.5 demonstrating the highest corrosion resistance (0.131 μA/cm2). Corrosion resistance decreased along with the content of copper because copper segregation accelerated local corrosion throughout the alloy.

Effects of Cold Rolling or Precipitation Hardening Treatment on the Microstructure, Mechanical Properties, and Corrosion Resistance of Ti-Rich Metastable Medium-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractTitanium-rich metastable medium-entropy alloys, designed for low elastic moduli, sacrifice strength. However, enhancing their mechanical strength is crucial for bio-implant applications. This study aims to enhance the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of a metastable Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 medium-entropy alloy using various treatments, including cold rolling (at 50% and 75% reduction) and precipitation hardening (at room temperature, 150 °C, 350 °C, 550 °C, and 750 °C). The results showed that the alloy underwent a stress-induced martensitic transformation during the rolling process. Notably, the α phase was precipitated in the β grain boundaries after 30 days of precipitation hardening at room temperature. The yield strengths of the alloy increased by 51% and 281.9% after room-temperature precipitation and 75% cold rolling, respectively. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment.
